title: COIL en sistemas inalámbricos MIMO-BICM (Nivel 1)
note: Caso trazado paso a paso en la Sección IV del paper. Observa cómo se preservan 1.3dB, 0.8dB, LMMSE, COIL, MIMO e IDD.
text: In signal processing, BICM is commonly used in MIMO wireless systems, but there's a trade-off when it comes to MIMO data detection and channel decoding. We're looking at the problem where we only share per-bit soft info, which doesn't account for the correlation between bits in each transmitted vector. This gap in information can really mess with the performance of one-shot receivers. Sure, IDD can handle most of this deficiency, but it's not great for complexity or delay. Here's our fix - we're working on COIL, a new kind of soft-output that factors in per-bit info plus pairwise coupling logits for related bits. By tweaking this into a traditional belief-propagation channel decoder, we're hoping to enable correlation-aware decoding in one shot without relying on IDD. In testing with a MIMO-BICM setup using low-density parity-check codes, our single-pass LMMSE receiver with COIL is beating the standard one-shot unbiased LMMSE receiver by 1.3dB. Plus, it's only about 0.8dB behind a four-iteration IDD receiver, and it does it all in one go.
reference: Bit-interleaved coded modulation (BICM) is widely used in multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) wireless systems. However, separating MIMO data detection from channel decoding and only exchanging per-bit soft information discards correlation information among the bits within each transmit vector. We show that the resulting information loss limits the performance of practical one-shot receivers. Even though iterative detection and decoding (IDD) can recover most of this loss, IDD significantly increases receiver complexity and latency. In order to reduce this loss, we propose COrrelation-Informed Logits (COIL), a soft-output format that combines per-bit soft information with pairwise coupling logits for correlated bits. We show how to incorporate these coupling logits into a conventional belief-propagation-based channel decoder, which enables correlation-aware decoding in a one-shot receiver without IDD. We evaluate COIL in a MIMO-BICM system with a conventional low-density parity-check code. For a 4x4 MIMO orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) system, a one-shot linear minimum mean-square error (LMMSE) receiver with COIL outperforms a conventional one-shot unbiased LMMSE receiver by 1.3dB and operates within 0.8dB of four-iteration IDD, while requiring only a single pass through the data detector.

title: COIL con saludo coloquial extremo ('Hey there! ...')
note: Prueba de fuego de Nivel 3 (Tabla IX): la línea base suele responder con saludos epistolares ('Dear Colleague,' o 'Certainly...'), mientras P-PAP-v1 los elimina al 0%.
text: Hey there! So, you know how we always use BICM with MIMO stuff for wireless systems, right? Well, here's the thing: when we separate data detection from channel decoding and just swap per-bit soft info, we kinda lose some of the cool correlations between bits in each transmission vector. And that's bad news for how well one-shot receivers do. But hey, there's this thing called IDD that can bring back a lot of that lost goodness. The downside? It makes things way more complex and slow. So, we came up with this nifty thing called COIL. It's a new way to handle soft-output that mixes up the per-bit soft info with these thingies called pairwise coupling logits. It's all about keeping that bit correlation in check. We've even figured out how to slam these logits into a regular belief-propagation channel decoder. This means we can decode with all the correlation jazz in a single shot, without the need for IDD. Plus, when we tested it out in a MIMO-BICM setup using a LDPC code, our COIL-powered one-shot LMMSE receiver nailed it. It's beating the old-school unbiased version by a solid 1.3dB, and it's chilling just 0.8dB away from what you'd get after four rounds of IDD. The best part? It only needs to go through the data detector once. Pretty cool, huh?

title: Detector YOLOv8 en Raspberry Pi 4 (94.2% F1, 28 fps, 4.5 W)
note: Borrador corto de validación de despliegue local. Verifica conservación exacta de hardware, métrica, tasa de cuadros y potencia eléctrica.
text: We built a YOLOv8 detector on a Raspberry Pi 4 that hits 94.2% F1-score at 28 fps while drawing only 4.5 W during continuous outdoor edge inference, beating our previous MobileNetV2 baseline by 6.1% without needing an external Coral TPU.

title: Spiking-FullSubNet neuromórfico en FPGA PYNQ-Z1
note: Borrador redactado manualmente por humano tras lectura única: incluye 52.9nJ, 32ms, 45nm, PYNQ-Z1, 0.727 y 100MHz.
text: The work intends to solve via neuromorphic computing the power consumption in devices like smartphones, wireless headphones and hearing aids when using audio denoising neural networks. Though SNNs can potentially solve the problem thanks to their high activation sparsity and low complecity, many SOTA SNN's won't perform inference to its fullest without hardware that supports a mixture of operations. We can solve this by converting SOTA audio denoising neural network Spiking-FullSubNet to a hardware friendly version, which means QAT and simplifying function activation can achieve 28x improvement in power consumption to 52.9nJ per 32ms audio frame when calculated for custom digital hardware in a 45nm process node. Then, a digital circuit that can perform inference of the heterogeneous compute load of Spiking-FullSubNet with a sparsity-aware flexible PE array is proposed, so we can validate this circuit on a PYNQ-Z1 FPGA and finally achieve a real-time factor of 0.727 at 100MHz.
reference: In this work we look to neuromorphic computing to solve the power consumption problem that audio denoising neural networks face on edge devices like smartphones, wireless headphones and hearing aids. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) have the potential to solve this problem due to their high activation sparsity and low complexity, however many SOTA SNNs require hardware that supports a mixture of operations to be able to fully perform inference. To solve this problem, we convert SOTA audio denoising neural network Spiking-FullSubNet to a hardware friendly version showing that via QAT and activation function simplification we can achieve $\approx28\times$ improvement in power consumption to 52.9nJ per 32ms audio frame when calculated for custom digital hardware in a 45nm process node. We then propose a digital circuit which by means of a sparsity-aware flexible PE array can perform inference of the heterogeneous compute load of Spiking-FullSubNet, and validate this circuit on a PYNQ-Z1 FPGA achieving a real-time factor of 0.727 at 100MHz.

title: Comunicaciones críticas 5G + Satélite NTN (Open5GS)
note: Caso humano con 100% de cobertura y preservación exacta de unidades en Tabla VI (60.03 ms, 9.42 puntos, 184.52 ms).
text: Public mobile networks may present many problems during disasters, so deployable communication systems are required to support emergency operations. This is why the article proposes a mission-critical communications system supporing MCPTT, MCVideo and MCData over a private 5G standaloe network with NTN connectivity. A context-aware QPP mechanism might dynamically adapt network resource allocation according to the operational state of MCX. Extensions to the Open5GS PCF and SMF enable priority and pre-emption updates for existing flows without session re-establishment. This architecture can both support tactical edge deployment of service and media functions and, at the same time, retain centralized service control. Three configurations are considered when evaluating via experiments: terrestrial backhaul with centralized media processing, satellite backhaul with centralized media processing, and satellite backhaul with edge media processing. Main results are that tactical edge processing reduces communication delay and packet loss; under satellite backhaul, edge processing reduced the 95th-percentile MCPTT audio transport delay by 60.03 ms and packet loss by 9.42 percentage points, while achieving a 95th-percentile MCPTT access time of 184.52 ms. These results show the benefits of tactical edge media processing and provide foundation for context-aware priority mechanisms in public-safety networks that integrate terrestrial and non-terrestrial components.
reference: During disasters, public mobile networks may become unavailable, congested, or degraded, requiring deployable communication systems to support emergency operations. This article proposes a mission-critical communications system supporing Mission Critical Push-to-Talk (MCPTT), Mission Critical Video (MCVideo), and Mission Critical Data (MCData) over a private 5G standalone network with Non-Terrestrial Network (NTN) connectivity. A context-aware Quality, Priority, and Pre-emption (QPP) mechanism is proposed to dynamically adapt network resource allocation according to the operational state of Mission Critical Services (MCX). Extensions to the Open5GS Policy Control Function (PCF) and Session Management Function (SMF) enable priority and pre-emption updates for existing flows without session re-establishment. The architecture supports tactical edge deployment of service and media functions while retaining centralized service control. Experimental evaluation considers three configurations: terrestrial backhaul with centralized media processing, satellite backhaul with centralized media processing, and satellite backhaul with edge media processing. Results show that tactical edge processing reduces communication delay and packet loss. Under satellite backhaul, edge processing reduced the 95th-percentile MCPTT audio transport delay by 60.03 ms and packet loss by 9.42 percentage points, while achieving a 95th-percentile MCPTT access time of 184.52 ms. These findings demonstrate the benefits of tactical edge media processing and provide an experimental foundation for context-aware priority mechanisms in public-safety networks integrating terrestrial and non-terrestrial components.

title: Lente de onda milimétrica a 100 GHz (coma hispana '11,9 mm')
note: Caso destacado en Sección V.C: el redactor humano escribió coma decimal hispana '11,9 mm' y P-PAP-v1 la normalizó correctamente al estándar inglés '11.9 mm'.
text: This article presents a new method to turn a millimetre-wave source with a Gaussian distribution into a flat-top by using a single curved surface. The lens is designed to operate at 100 GHz and is placed 52 mm in front of a conical horn antenna. The wave then goes from 11,9 mm to 400 mm. The lens profile is optimised through electromagnetic simulation to prove its success. And the sensitivity to frequency changes is investigated.
reference: This paper presents a novel method for converting the divergent Gaussian intensity distribution of a millimeter-wave source into a uniform (flat-top) distribution using a single curved surface. The proposed method combines the surface profile of a collimator with that of a beam shaper. To validate the method, the profile of a single-sided (plano-convex) lens is derived and placed 52 mm in front of a conical horn antenna operating at 100 GHz. The lens transforms the Gaussian radiation of the horn, with an incident beam radius of 11.9 mm, into a uniform beam with a radius of 400 mm at a distance of 3 m. The lens surface profile is optimized using a full-wave-simulation-based procedure, and the resulting output beam is compared with that of a previously designed double-sided (concave-convex) lens. Simulation results show that, within the desired field of view, the optimized single-sided lens produces a flat-top intensity distribution with satisfactory ripple and roll-off. Finally, the sensitivity of the optimized lens to frequency variation is investigated. The proposed lens is suitable for generating uniform illumination in active stand-off millimeter-wave imaging systems.

title: Cooperación aire-tierra UAV–UGV bajo incertidumbre de mapa
note: Borrador sintético aprobado por el filtro (keep=true) con métricas 98.9%, 87.7%, 2.94 seconds y 2 km.
text: In our systems and control field, we're tackling the issue of when our UGV needs a lift and what the UAV should look at. We're putting together a plan that's all about the map uncertainties and how they mess with our UGV's navigation. Basically, we score different map scenarios and pick the one that's gonna make our UGV's path smoother. Once we've got that map, we get aerial data, mix it in, and come up with a new plan. We're doing things differently, focusing on if resolving these uncertainties actually helps our UGV move better. In our 180 trial runs, we nailed 98.9% of the goals and cut down our UAV flight time by a massive 87.7%. On average, every second we save in flight time means we're saving our UGV 2.94 seconds on the ground. Plus, our field tests over 2 km show that our method's really effective at fixing things when there's uncertainty.
reference: Heterogeneous air-ground teams can use aerial sensing to address the limited range and viewpoint of ground-vehicle sensors, but deciding when the UGV needs assistance and what information the UAV should collect remains a challenge. This paper presents a planner-conditioned air-ground assistance method that evaluates how uncertain map information affects the UGV's current MPPI rollouts. When navigation remains degraded, we score the same rollouts under resolved map hypotheses, select the map layer with the largest useful improvement, request the corresponding aerial measurement, fuse the returned information, and replan. Unlike approaches driven by fixed support roles, task structure, or uncertainty alone, our method conditions assistance on whether resolving uncertainty improves predicted ground navigation. Across 180 simulation trials on three off-road routes, the method achieves 98.9% goal attainment while reducing mean UAV flight time by 87.7% relative to continuous greedy aerial mapping. Aggregated across the routes, each second of estimated UAV flight time saves 2.94 s of UGV navigation time. Field experiments spanning approximately 2 km of UGV operation demonstrate uncertainty resolution and successful navigation recovery.

cat: eess.IV · Imagen y Video Radar SAR
title: Estabilidad radiométrica del radar SAR banda P BIOMASS
note: Borrador sintético con acrónimos de dominio aeroespacial (BIOMASS, SAR, PSCal, PSs, RFI) y cifras en decibeles (1 dB, 0.1 dB).
text: We dove into the world of image and video processing for the European Space Agency's BIOMASS P-band SAR, where keeping things steady's key. We wanted to suss out how we could tell the difference between instrument changes and actual scene changes without needing extra calibration gear. Our go-to method, the PSCal thingy, uses PSs to estimate how much the radiometric stuff needs adjusting. We ran some simulations to check how well it works, especially when we only got a handful of data chunks, and we found we really need to be picky about our selection thresholds. When we tested this out in Nairobi, we stumbled upon a 1 dB oddity, which we think is due to some RFI issues. Most of the time, though, the changes we got were within 0.1 dB. Then we hit Cordoba, where we had twelve bits of info over eight months. Even with big scene and acquisition shape changes, we only saw about 0.1 dB variations. Our finds matched up with the BIOMASS CAL Transponder readings from New Norcia. So, it seems like our careful picking of P-band PSs could be a real game-changer for keeping track of radiometric shifts and spotting glitches.
reference: Monitoring the relative radiometric stability of the European Space Agency's BIOMASS P-band synthetic aperture radar (SAR) requires separating instrumental and processing effects from temporal changes in the scene backscatter. This study investigates the use of permanent scatterers (PSs) as opportunistic references for estimating residual radiometric gains without dedicated calibration targets. The PS-based calibration (PSCal) framework combines amplitude-based scatterer selection with iterative maximum-likelihood gain estimation. Simulations assess detection and estimation performance under the limited number of acquisitions available in BIOMASS stacks, highlighting the importance of stringent selection thresholds and the dependence of estimation accuracy on scatterer abundance and signal-to-noise ratio. The approach is applied to datasets over Nairobi, Kenya, and Cordoba, Argentina. Over Nairobi, PSCal identifies an approximately 1 dB radiometric anomaly subsequently traced to a defect in radio-frequency interference mitigation, while the remaining acquisitions exhibit estimated gain variations generally within 0.1 dB. Over Cordoba, twelve acquisitions spanning two mission phases separated by approximately eight months yield residual gain variations on the order of 0.1 dB despite pronounced changes in the scene backscatter and acquisition geometry. Results were observed to be consistent with measurements from the BIOMASS Calibration Transponder (BCT) installed in New Norcia (Australia). These results demonstrate the potential of carefully selected P-band PSs to complement dedicated calibration infrastructure for relative radiometric monitoring and the detection of processing anomalies.
